newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO set for success with global infotech agreement.
newsitem.headline: WTO set for success with global infotech agreement.

text.p: A ground-breaking agreement on Thursday to free global commerce in information technology swept the World Trade Organisation (WTO) towards a triumphant inaugural meeting.

The Information Technology Agreement, reached after four days of intense, round-the-clock talks, marked the most far-reaching agreement towards free trade in a single sector and should slash prices not only on high-technology but on goods from cars to copiers to washing machines.

But wrangling among trade ministers over whether the WTO should be involved in improving workers' standards and should further liberalise agriculture markets threatened a final declaration that must be completed by the close of the meeting on Friday.

Envoys had viewed a deal between the United States and the European Union to scrap tariffs on billions of dollars of information technology trade by the year 2000 as a target to mark the real success of the meeting and a reward to months of hard diplomatic driving by the United States.
Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said the benefits to world trade would far exceed the financial savings from tariff reductions.
"The extent of tariff savings, which I guess would be quite hefty, doesn't begin to measure the ultimate economic benefits of agreements of this sort," she said.

"This is the biggest trade step forward...that has happened since the end of the Uruguay Round," EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said, referring to the largest set of measures ever adopted to liberalise world trade and completed in 1993.
"It will be good for the IT industry, and will act as a catalyst for industrial growth," he said. "As such it will be good for the whole world economy."

The breakthrough came when Brittan won endorsement from the 15-member European Union Council for a compromise deal seen as boosting U.S. corporate profits and benefiting many of Asia's tiger economies. Europe stood to lose most since it has among the highest tariff levels in the world.

European officials said final agreement still depended on enough countries -- those representing about 90 percent of world trade in the sector -- joining the pact by March 15, 1997. They saw 85 percent signing the agreement by Friday.
Many Asian members have indicated support for the deal, but want flexibility over the timing of the tariff cuts.

Compromise between the United States and Europe produced a deal covering the bulk of industrial information technology products, as well as digital photocopiers and capacitors -- circuits used in electronic equipment-- while excluding consumer electronics and audio materials.
But Third World development groups warned that "corporate greed" was winning out at the conference, leaving poor people round the globe to suffer.

Differences over the contentious issues of discussion in the WTO of competition and investment policies and the way national authorities award contracts, or government procurement, had been resolved this week, officials said.
"Whoever would have said a week ago we would have agreement there?" said one senior diplomat.

However, battles on agriculture and a link between trade and labour standards that is seen by developing countries as a U.S.-backed protectionist ploy were giving rise to fierce debate and holding up the final declaration.
"The position is still fluid. I can't say whether there will be agreement tonight or tomorrow," said Indian Commerce Secretary Tejendra Khanna.
India was one of the countries that began the conference, which operates by consensus, saying it did not want to see any mention of labour in the final declaration.

The United States has been adamant that the issue should be included in the declaration, effectively the WTO agenda, to try to address voters' concerns over 250 million child labourers, mostly in the developing world, and sweatshop conditions.
WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero was upbeat. "The discussion is continuing but the atmosphere is good," he told reporters.
